newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S.-Colombia at rockbottom, U.S. envoy says.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Colombia at rockbottom, U.S. envoy says.

text.p: U.S. ambassador Myles Frechette blamed Colombia's dire record on drug trafficking, corruption and human rights for pushing relations with the United States to their lowest level since the Second World War, in an interview published on Sunday.

The extensive article, published in the leading daily El Tiempo, came just two days after Colombia's billionaire cocaine kings, Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, were sentenced to jail terms that will see them walk free in just five years.
Frechette's outspoken remarks have in the past aroused the ire of Colombian politicians for what they see as his meddling in internal affairs.

His latest interview, in a newspaper which has been harshly critical of President Ernesto Samper's administration, appears to be a calculated decision to send Colombia one of his toughest messages yet.
Many of the same comments were made "off the record" to foreign correspondents at a press briefing Friday but the envoy gave only El Tiempo permission to publish a full "on the record" interview.

"It would be correct to say that (relations are at their most tense) since the Second World War...the fact that (the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers) can run their businesses from jail amounts to the Colombian government backing drug trafficking," the U.S. envoy said.

The Rodriguezes, former chieftains of the mighty Cali drug Cartel, were granted maximum sentence reductions by an anonymous, or "faceless." judge after admitting their role in creating a worldwide criminal empire and smuggling tons of cocaine into the United States.

The ruling, which Frechette described as "lamentable", appears to have torpedoed all hopes of Colombia overturning its status as an international drug pariah and regaining certification as a U.S. ally in the drug war this March.
While admitting that he often "shared a joke" with Samper, Frechette took at sideswipe at the president and the country's political classes.

"We're disappointed because, without doubt, not enough has been done to combat corruption," he said. U.S.-Colombian relations were rocked early on in the current administration when Samper was accused of funding his 1994 election camapign with Cali cartel cash.
He was later cleared by Congress but the United States withdrew his U.S. entry visa, citing his known ties with prominent drug lords.

Frechette spelled out in the interview that Colombia could only boost its chances of regaining certification if Congress lifted the country's ban on extradition, approved tougher sentences for drug crimes and granted U.S. officials the right to board Colombian vessels to search for illicit drug consignments.

He also sounded a warning on Colombia's human rights record, one of the worst in Latin America, saying: "The United States has noted with great concern the increase in the number of human rights violations...Ambassador Juan Carlos Esguerra (Colombia's new envoy to Washington) is going to have a very tough time explaining things," Frechette added.

International human rights groups, Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, however, both accused the United States of fuelling the level of violations by the Colombian army and right- wing paramilitaries and called for a halt to U.S. arms sales to Colombia in reports late last year. Washington rejected the call.
